Finding things out

A record can forget completely.

Once a record leaves out a difference, that record may be unable to recover it.

A closer lookOpen the shared interactive reader ↗

The interactive example has its own motion control. Scroll inside it if you need more room.

A mathematical limit on what a record can tell us

The pairs 1 and 3, or 2 and 2, both add up to 4. If the only record is the sum, you cannot tell which pair it came from.

Keep the first number as a second record and you can tell these pairs apart. That uses new information. It does not recover the answer from the sum alone.

Try both pairs. Then keep a second record and see what becomes clear.

Words used here
record
The information that was kept. A record may leave out differences that were present in the original event.
Read the fuller explanation

Take two labelled pairs: one and three, or two and two. A detector that keeps only their sum reports four for both. You cannot tell which pair occurred from that sum alone. Repeating the same arithmetic does not recover the missing label.

Add a second record that retains the first coordinate and the pair becomes identifiable in this tiny declared family. You have enriched the record; you have not extracted the answer from the original sum.

The corpus’s recovery boundary is strict: not every reduction leaves a recoverable remnant of everything it removes. A truthful account can finish by naming what the available theory cannot tell you. That limit is useful knowledge.

Where this comes from: What a record cannot recover

Exact information boundary · scoped recovery

A mathematical limit on what a record can tell us

If two origins leave exactly the same record, that record alone cannot tell them apart. A second, different record can help.

Read the full source note

No universal scar and the recovery boundary

States in the same detector fibre cannot be distinguished using only functions of that retained record. Recovery requires an additional distinguishing record or a richer theory. The dot-and-sum example is an authored finite illustration.
